newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutors rest case in Oklahoma City bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors rest case in Oklahoma City bomb trial.

text.p: Prosecutors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial rested their case on Wednesday after presenting 137 witnesses in 18 days to tie Timothy McVeigh to the worst attack on civilians in U.S. history.
"On behalf of the United States, we are pleased to announce that we rest," chief prosecutor Joseph Hartzler said in court.

The prosecution knit a web of circumstantial evidence against McVeigh, the decorated Gulf War veteran who is charged with blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people. It raced through its case far more quickly than expected.
After the jury was dismissed, chief defence lawyer Stephen Jones filed a motion to dismiss the charges against McVeigh on the grounds the prosecution had failed to prove its case.

Federal Judge Richard Matsch denied the motion, which is routinely filed by the defence in criminal cases, but he reserved judgment on other defence motions to delete parts of the indictment against McVeigh.

Jones said prosecutors had failed to prove allegations in the indictment that McVeigh bought 2,000 pounds (907 kg) of ammonium nitrate or that the bomb was built at a state park in Kansas. Ammonium nitrate was a key component of the bomb, the prosecution says.
Matsch indicated he was sympathetic to the defence, saying he was considering editing or even making more substantial changes to the indictment before it was given to the jury.
Jones said the defence would call its first witness on Thursday, but did not say how long he would take to present his case.
The government says McVeigh, 29, bombed the federal building to avenge the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a clash with federal agents at Waco, Texas, exactly two years earlier.
He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murder and conspiracy but could face the death penalty if convicted.

Prosecution witnesses have testified that McVeigh talked about bombing the federal building and shopped for bomb materials. A witness identified McVeigh as the man who rented the Ryder truck allegedly used in the bombing and an FBI scientist said he found traces of explosives on McVeigh's clothes.
But there were gaps in the prosecution case. No one placed McVeigh in Oklahoma City on the day of the bombing and his fingerprints were not found on key evidence.

The prosecution put three final witnesses on the stand on Wednesday to drive home the human tragedy of the blast -- a survivor, a rescuer and Fred Jordan, the medical examiner for state of Oklahoma whose office identified the bodies.
McVeigh sat impassively through most of the court session, smiling once at a lighter moment.

Florence Rogers, chief executive of the Federal Employees Credit Union on the third floor of the Murrah building, described in a low voice how seven women employees she was meeting with in her office were blown away by the blast.
"When I was able to stand up, all of the girls in my office had totally disappeared, with the six floors up above us on top of them. I never saw them again," Rogers said.

Relatives of bombing victims sobbed as Rogers gravely read out the names of the 18 employees of the credit union who were killed in the blast and pointed out on a floor plan where they were when she last saw them.

Mike Shannon, special operations chief of the Oklahoma City Fire Department and one of the first emergency workers on the scene, told how a bomb scare forced rescuers to leave the building 90 minutes after the blast, leaving four or five survivors trapped inside.

The bomb scare was caused by a desk clock shaped like a "TV comic strip bomb," he said. Someone spotted the clock -- belonging to an agent of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms -- which had been knocked into the stairwell, and raised the alarm. People were very nervous at the time, fearing there could be a second explosion.
